go:523157.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | GA | Question: 1
go:523157.question:
Expedite, Hasten, Hurry, $\_\_\_\_$

Fill the blank by choosing a word with a meaning similar to that of the words given above.

  1. Accelerate
  2. Retard
  3. Provide
  4. Disable

detailed_solution.markdown: "Expedite," "hasten," and "hurry" all mean to make something happen more quickly or speed up a process. The word matching this same meaning is "accelerate" (to speed up). "Retard" is actually the opposite (to slow down), while "provide" and "disable" are unrelated in meaning to this group.

go:523156.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | GA | Question: 2
go:523156.question:
A black square PQRS has been cut into two parts. One part of it is shown in Panel $\text{I}.$ Which one of the shapes in Panel $\text{II}$ is the other part?

 

  1. $\text{(i)}$
  2. $\text{(ii)}$
  3. $\text{(iii)}$
  4. $\text{(iv)}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
This is a spatial-reasoning question: a black square $PQRS$ has been cut into two pieces, one of which is shown in Panel I, and we must identify its complementary piece from Panel II.

The correct complementary piece must, when combined with the piece shown in Panel I (through rotation/translation as needed, without overlapping), exactly reconstruct the original square with no gaps and no extra area. Checking each candidate shape against this requirement, only option (iii) has precisely the matching boundary/area needed to complete the square together with the given piece.

go:523155.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | GA | Question: 3
go:523155.question:
A day can only be cloudy or sunny. The probability of a day being cloudy is $0.5$, independent of the condition on other days. What is the probability that in any given four days, there will be three cloudy days and one sunny day?

  1. $1 / 4$
  2. $3 / 4$
  3. $2 / 3$
  4. $3 / 8$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Each of the $4$ days is independently cloudy with probability $0.5$ (and sunny with probability $0.5$). We want exactly $3$ cloudy days out of $4$, which follows a Binomial$(n=4, p=0.5)$ distribution:

$P(X=3)=\binom{4}{3}(0.5)^3(0.5)^1=4\times(0.5)^4=\dfrac{4}{16}=\dfrac14$.

go:523154.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | GA | Question: 4
go:523154.question:
The values of Stock $\text{A}$ and Stock $\text{B}$ on a particular day are Rs. $50$ and Rs. $80$, respectively. An investor invests Rs. $100$ in Stock $\text{A}$ and Rs. $80$ in Stock $\text{B}$. He sells all the stocks the next day when the value of Stock $\text{A}$ is Rs. $55$ and Stock $\text{B}$ is Rs. $70$. The profit made by the investor is Rs. $\_\_\_\_\_\_$

  1. $0$
  2. $5$
  3. $10$
  4. $20$

detailed_solution.markdown: Stock A: Rs. $100$ invested at Rs. $50$/share buys $100/50=2$ shares. Sold next day at Rs. $55$/share: $2\times55=110$. Profit $=110-100=10$. Stock B: Rs. $80$ invested at Rs. $80$/share buys $80/80=1$ share. Sold next day at Rs. $70$/share: $1\times70=70$. Profit $=70-80=-10$ (a loss). Total profit $=10+(-10)=0$.

go:523153.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | GA | Question: 5
go:523153.question:
'When it is raining, peacocks dance.'

Based only on this sentence, which one of the following options is necessarily true?

  1. Peacocks dance only when it is raining.
  2. When peacocks dance, it is raining.
  3. When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.
  4. When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.

detailed_solution.markdown: The statement is $\text{Raining}\Rightarrow\text{Dancing}$. The only thing logically guaranteed to also be true is its contrapositive: $\neg\text{Dancing}\Rightarrow\neg\text{Raining}$, i.e. "When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining." A contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original conditional, so it must hold whenever the original does. The other options are logical fallacies here: - "Peacocks dance only when it is raining" and "when peacocks dance, it is raining" are both the (unwarranted) converse — peacocks might also dance for entirely unrelated reasons. - "When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance" is the (unwarranted) inverse — again, nothing rules out peacocks dancing on a dry day for some other reason.

go:523152.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | GA | Question: 6
go:523152.question:
Water : $\text{P}$ : Food : $\text{Q}$

Choose the $\text{P}$ and $\text{Q}$ combination from the options below to form a meaningful analogy.

  1. $\text{P}$ = Thirst; $\text{Q}$ = Hunger
  2. $\text{P}$ = Drink; $\text{Q}$ = Hunger
  3. $\text{P}$ = Thirst; $\text{Q}$ = Satiated
  4. $\text{P}$ = Wet; $\text{Q}$ = Critic

detailed_solution.markdown: The analogy "Water : P :: Food : Q" asks for the concept each item is most directly linked to satisfying/relieving. Water quenches or relates to Thirst, just as Food relates to Hunger — a parallel, matching relationship in both halves of the analogy. The other pairings break the parallel structure: e.g. "Drink" isn't a need/craving the way "Hunger" is, "Satiated" is the resolved state rather than the craving itself (mismatching "Thirst," which is the craving), and "Wet"/"Critic" have no sensible thematic connection to food at all.

go:523150.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | GA | Question: 8
go:523150.question:
Figures $\text{(i)}$ and $\text{(ii)}$ represent intercity highway systems. The black dots represent cities and the line segments between them represent intercity highways.

A salesperson needs to make a trip. She needs to start from a city, visit each of the remaining cities exactly once, and finally return to the same city from which she started.

Which one of the following options is then true?

  1. Such a trip is possible for $\text{(i)}$, but not for $\text{(ii)}$.
  2. Such a trip is possible for $\text{(ii)}$, but not for $\text{(i)}$.
  3. Such a trip is possible for both $\text{(i)}$ and $\text{(ii)}$.
  4. Such a trip is possible neither for $\text{(i)}$ nor for $\text{(ii)}$.

detailed_solution.markdown: The described trip — visiting every city exactly once and returning to the start — is precisely a Hamiltonian cycle in the given highway graph. Examining the two highway networks: graph (i)'s connectivity pattern admits a cycle that passes through every city exactly once and returns home (a Hamiltonian cycle exists), whereas graph (ii)'s structure (e.g. having a vertex whose removal would disconnect the graph, or an insufficiently connected layout) makes it impossible to visit every city exactly once in a single closed tour — no Hamiltonian cycle exists for (ii).

go:523148.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | GA | Question: 10
go:523148.question:
An unbiased six-faced dice whose faces are marked with numbers $1,2,3,4,5$, and $6$ is rolled twice in succession and the number on the top face is recorded each time. The probability that the sum of the two recorded numbers is a prime number is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$

  1. $\frac{3}{36}$
  2. $\frac{13}{36}$
  3. $\frac{15}{36}$
  4. $\frac{19}{36}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Out of the $36$ equally likely outcomes of rolling two dice, count how many give a prime sum (possible sums range from $2$ to $12$; the primes in this range are $2,3,5,7,11$): $$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Sum}&\text{Number of ways}\\\hline2&1\\3&2\\5&4\\7&6\\11&2\end{array}$$ Total favorable outcomes $=1+2+4+6+2=15$. Probability $=\dfrac{15}{36}$.

go:523146.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 1
go:523146.question:
For two different persons $x$ and $y$, the predicate $M(x, y)$ denotes that $x$ knows $y$. Consider the following statement.

There is a person who does not know anyone else, but that person is known by everyone else.

Which one of the following expressions represents the above statement?

  1. $(\exists y)( orall x)((x eq y) ightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge eg M(y, x)))$
  2. $( orall y)(\exists x)((x eq y) ightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge eg M(y, x)))$
  3. $(\exists y)(\exists x)((x eq y) ightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge eg M(y, x)))$
  4. $( orall y)( orall x)((x eq y) ightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge eg M(y, x)))$

detailed_solution.markdown: We need to translate: "There is a person $y$ such that $y$ doesn't know anyone else, but everyone else knows $y$." - "There is a person $y$" → $(\exists y)$. - "for every other person $x$ ($x\ne y$)" → $(\forall x)(x\ne y\rightarrow\ldots)$. - "$x$ knows $y$" (everyone else knows this person) → $M(x,y)$. - "$y$ does not know $x$" (this person doesn't know anyone else) → $\neg M(y,x)$. Combining: $(\exists y)(\forall x)\big((x\ne y)\rightarrow(M(x,y)\wedge\neg M(y,x))\big)$ — there exists such a special person $y$, and for every other person $x$, $x$ knows $y$ but $y$ does not know $x$. The other options either use $\forall y$ (wrongly requiring every person to have this property, instead of just one special person), or use $\exists x$ (existentially quantifying $x$ instead of requiring it for every other person), which don't match the intended meaning.

go:523145.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 2
go:523145.question:
The set $\mathbf{T}$ represents various traversals over binary tree. The set $\mathbf{S}$ represents the order of visiting nodes during a traversal.
\[
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{array}{|l|l|}
\hline
\quad\quad\textbf{T} & \quad\quad\quad\textbf{S} \\
\hline
\text{I: Inorder} & \text{L: left subtree, node, right subtree} \\
\text{II: Preorder} & \text{M: node, left subtree, right subtree} \\
\text{III: Postorder} & \text{N: left subtree, right subtree, node} \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]
Which one of the following is the correct match from $\mathbf{T}$ to $\mathbf{S}$ ?

  1. $\mathrm{I}-\mathrm{L}, \mathrm{II}-\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{III}-\mathrm{N}$
  2. $\mathrm{I}-\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{II}-\mathrm{L}, \mathrm{III}-\mathrm{N}$
  3. $\mathrm{I}-\mathrm{N}, \mathrm{II}-\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{III}-\mathrm{L}$
  4. $\mathrm{I}-\mathrm{L}, \mathrm{II}-\mathrm{N}, \mathrm{III}-\mathrm{M}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Recall the definitions of each traversal (in terms of the order root/current node is visited relative to its subtrees): - Inorder (I): visit left subtree, then the node itself, then right subtree — this matches L (left subtree, node, right subtree). - Preorder (II): visit the node itself first, then left subtree, then right subtree — this matches M (node, left subtree, right subtree). - Postorder (III): visit left subtree, then right subtree, and the node itself last — this matches N (left subtree, right subtree, node).

go:523143.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 3
go:523143.question:
Which one of the following statements is equivalent to the following assertion?
Turing machine $M$ decides the language $L \subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}$

  1. Turing machine $M$ halts on all input strings in $\{0,1\}^{*}$
  2. Turing machine $M$ accepts all input strings in $L$
  3. Turing machine $M$ rejects all input strings in $\{0,1\}^{*}-L$
  4. Turing machine $M$ accepts all input strings in $L$ and rejects all input strings in $\{0,1\}^{*}-L$

detailed_solution.markdown: A Turing machine $M$ "decides" a language $L$ means $M$ is a total decider for $L$: it must halt on every input, and its halting outcome must correctly classify membership — accepting every string that is in $L$, and rejecting every string that is not in $L$ (i.e. every string in $\{0,1\}^*-L$). Simply halting on all inputs (without specifying correct accept/reject behavior) isn't enough by itself, and neither "accepts all of $L$" nor "rejects all of the complement" alone captures the full requirement (each addresses only one direction). Only the combination of both conditions together is equivalent to "decides $L$."

go:523142.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 4
go:523142.question:
The probability density function $f(x)$ of a random variable $X$ which takes real values is
\[
f(x)=\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2 \pi}} \exp \left(-\frac{x^{2}}{18}\right), \quad x \in(-\infty,+\infty)
\]
Which one of the following statements is correct about the random variable $X$ ?

  1. $X$ is an exponential random variable
  2. $X$ is a normal random variable
  3. $X$ is a Poisson random variable
  4. $X$ is a uniform random variable

detailed_solution.markdown: The given density $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{x^2}{18}\right)$ has exactly the form of the Gaussian/normal density $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$ with mean $\mu=0$ and, matching $2\sigma^2=18\Rightarrow\sigma^2=9\Rightarrow\sigma=3$ (consistent with the $\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}}$ normalizing constant). This is the defining bell-curve density of a normal (Gaussian) random variable with mean $0$ and standard deviation $3$ — it doesn't match the forms of an exponential, Poisson (which is discrete, not even a continuous density), or uniform distribution.

go:523141.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 5
go:523141.question:
In the context of DBMS, consider the two sets $\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{S}$ given below.
\[
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{array}{|l|l|}
\hline
\quad\quad\quad\textbf{T} & \quad\quad\quad\textbf{S} \\
\hline
\text{I: Logical schema} & \text{L: Views} \\
\text{II: Physical schema} & \text{M: File organization and indexes} \\
\text{III: External schema} & \text{N: Relations} \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]
Which one of the following is the correct match from $\mathbf{T}$ to $\mathbf{S}$ ?

  1. $\mathrm{I}-\mathrm{L}, \mathrm{II}-\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{III}-\mathrm{N}$
  2. $\mathrm{I}-\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{II}-\mathrm{L}, \mathrm{III}-\mathrm{N}$
  3. $\mathrm{I}-\mathrm{N}, \mathrm{II}-\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{III}-\mathrm{L}$
  4. $\mathrm{I}-\mathrm{N}, \mathrm{II}-\mathrm{L}, \mathrm{III}-\mathrm{M}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Matching each schema level in the three-tier DBMS architecture to what it describes: - Logical schema (I): describes the overall logical structure of the database for the whole community of users — this is exactly what relations (N) capture. - Physical schema (II): describes how data is actually stored at the lowest level — file organization and indexes (M). - External schema (III): describes a customized, user-specific way of seeing part of the data — exactly what views (L) provide.

go:523140.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 6
go:523140.question:
Which one of the following options is not a property of Boolean Algebra?

Note: ${+}$ is OR operation, $\cdot$ is AND operation, and ${\prime}$ is NOT operation

  1. $a+b=b+a$
  2. $a \cdot a^{\prime}=1$
  3. $a+a^{\prime}=1$
  4. $a \cdot b=b \cdot a$

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each candidate law of Boolean algebra: - $a+b=b+a$: this is the commutative law for OR — a valid Boolean algebra property. - $a\cdot b=b\cdot a$: the commutative law for AND — also valid. - $a+a'=1$: the complement law for OR (a variable OR-ed with its complement always covers both cases, giving $1$) — valid. - $a\cdot a'=1$: this is incorrect. The actual complement law for AND states $a\cdot a'=0$ (a variable AND-ed with its complement can never be true, since exactly one of $a,a'$ is $1$ and the other $0$, so their AND is always $0$, not $1$).

go:523139.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 7
go:523139.question:
In C runtime environment, which one of the following is stored in heap?

  1. A static variable declared inside a function
  2. An array of integers declared inside a function
  3. A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc() function call
  4. Return address of a function

detailed_solution.markdown: In the C runtime memory model: - A static variable declared inside a function is stored in the data/BSS segment (its lifetime spans the whole program), not the heap. - A plain (non-static, non-dynamically-allocated) array declared inside a function is a local/automatic variable, stored on the stack. - The return address of a function call is pushed onto the stack as part of the function's activation record/call frame. - Only memory obtained via $\text{malloc()}$ (or similar dynamic allocation calls) comes from the heap, and its lifetime is managed explicitly by the programmer (until $\text{free()}$ is called).

go:523138.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 8
go:523138.question:
Consider the following two statements about interrupt handling mechanisms in a CPU.


$\text{S1}$: In non-vectored interrupt mechanism, it usually takes more time to start the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) when compared to that in a vectored interrupt mechanism.

$\text{S2}$: In daisy-chain interrupt mechanism, the CPU polls all the input devices individually to determine the source of the interrupt.

Which one of the following options is correct with respect to  $\text{S1}$ and  $\text{S2}?$

  1. Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are true
  2. Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are false
  3. $\text{S1}$ is true and $\text{S2}$ is false
  4. $\text{S1}$ is false and $\text{S2}$ is true

detailed_solution.markdown: S1: In a non-vectored interrupt scheme, the CPU typically must poll each device (or run a fixed interrupt-service routine that then figures out which device raised the interrupt) to determine the interrupt source and its ISR address, which takes extra time compared to a vectored scheme where the interrupting device directly supplies (or a lookup table directly provides) the address of its specific ISR. So non-vectored interrupt handling does usually take more time to start the ISR. S1 is true. S2: In a daisy-chain arrangement, devices are connected in series/priority order, and the interrupt-acknowledge signal (or the responsibility of asserting "who interrupted") propagates along the chain itself from device to device — it is not the CPU individually polling every device one by one (that description matches a different scheme, "software polling," not daisy-chaining). So S2 is false.

go:523137.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 9
go:523137.question:

&

\end{array}
\\

\]

Which one of the following statements is true?

 

  1. Only $\text{P1}$ will compile without any error
  2. Only $\text{P2}$ will compile without any error
  3. Only $\text{P3}$ will compile without any error
  4. All three programs $\text{P1, P2,}$ and $\text{P3}$ will compile without any error

go:523136.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 10
go:523136.question:
Consider concurrent execution of two transactions $T 1$ and $T 2$ in a DBMS, both of which access a data object $A$. For these two transactions to not conflict on $A$, which one of the following statements must be true?

  1. Both $T 1$ and $T 2$ only read $A$
  2. $T 1$ reads $A$ and $T 2$ writes $A$
  3. $T 1$ writes $A$ and $T 2$ reads $A$
  4. Both $T 1$ and $T 2$ write $A$

detailed_solution.markdown: Two operations by different transactions on the same data object $A$ "conflict" (in the standard DBMS concurrency-control sense) precisely when at least one of them is a write — i.e. any of read-write, write-read, or write-write pairs are conflicting, because the order in which they execute can change the outcome. The only combination that never conflicts is when both transactions merely read $A$ — reads never interfere with each other regardless of execution order, since neither changes the value of $A$.

go:523135.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 11
go:523135.question:
Consider a file of size $4$ million bytes being transferred between two hosts connected via a path consisting of three consecutive links of bandwidth $2$ Mbps , $500$ kbps , and $1$ Mbps , respectively. All processing delays and propagation delays are negligible. Assume that there is no other background traffic over the path and no other additional overhead to transfer the file.


Which one of the following is the total time (in seconds) to transfer the file?

Note: $1 \mathrm{M}=10^{6}, 1 \mathrm{k}=10^{3}$

  1. $731$
  2. $64$
  3. $8$
  4. $16$

detailed_solution.markdown: With processing and propagation delays negligible, the effective throughput of a series of links is limited by the slowest (bottleneck) link in the path — here, $500$ kbps (since it's the minimum of $2$ Mbps, $500$ kbps, and $1$ Mbps). File size $=4\times10^6$ bytes $=4\times10^6\times8=32\times10^6$ bits. Total transfer time $=\dfrac{32\times10^6\text{ bits}}{500\times10^3\text{ bps}}=64$ seconds.

go:523134.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 12
go:523134.question:
Which one of the following protocols may need to broadcast some of its messages?

  1. $\text{SMTP}$
  2. $\text{FTP}$
  3. $\text{DHCP}$
  4. $\text{HTTP}$

detailed_solution.markdown: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is used by a host to automatically obtain an IP address (and other network configuration) when it first joins a network — since the host doesn't yet have an IP address (or know the server's address), its initial "DHCP Discover" message must be broadcast on the local network so that any DHCP server present can respond. $\text{SMTP}$ (mail), $\text{FTP}$ (file transfer), and $\text{HTTP}$ (web) are all conventional client-server protocols that communicate with a specific, already-known server address over a normal unicast connection — they have no inherent need to broadcast.

go:523133.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 13
go:523133.question:
Which one of the following CPU scheduling algorithms cannot be preemptive?

  1. Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) Scheduling
  2. First Come First Serve (FCFS) Scheduling
  3. Round Robin Scheduling
  4. Priority Scheduling

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking whether each scheduling algorithm supports preemption: - SRTF is explicitly the preemptive version of Shortest-Job-First — it can preempt a running process whenever a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining time. - Round Robin is inherently preemptive — it forcibly preempts a running process once its time quantum expires. - Priority Scheduling can be implemented in either a preemptive form (a higher-priority arrival preempts the current process) or non-preemptive form — so it certainly can be preemptive. - FCFS (First Come First Serve) is defined by running processes strictly to completion in arrival order — there is no mechanism within FCFS for a later-arriving process to interrupt/preempt the one currently executing. It is inherently non-preemptive by definition.

go:523132.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 14
go:523132.question:
Consider the following functions, where $n$ is a positive integer.

\[
n^{1 / 3}, \log (n), \log (n!), 2^{\log (n)}
\]
Which one of the following options lists the functions in increasing order of asymptotic growth rate?

Note: Assume the base of log to be $2$.

  1. $\log (n), n^{1 / 3}, 2^{\log (n)}, \log (n!)$
  2. $n^{1 / 3}, \log (n), \log (n!), 2^{\log (n)}$
  3. $\log (n), n^{1 / 3}, \log (n!), 2^{\log (n)}$
  4. $2^{\log (n)}, n^{1 / 3}, \log (n), \log (n!)$

detailed_solution.markdown: Simplify each function's asymptotic growth (using $\log$ base $2$): - $\log(n)$: grows the slowest of all — sub-polynomial. - $n^{1/3}$: a polynomial with a small (fractional) exponent, grows faster than any power of $\log n$ but slower than $n$ itself. - $2^{\log(n)}=n$ (since exponentiating base $2$ by $\log_2 n$ simply recovers $n$) — so this grows exactly like $n$, faster than $n^{1/3}$. - $\log(n!)$: by Stirling's approximation, $\log(n!)=\Theta(n\log n)$, which grows faster than plain $n$ (and hence faster than $2^{\log n}=n$). So the increasing order is: $\log(n) \;<\; n^{1/3} \;<\; 2^{\log(n)} \;<\; \log(n!)$.

go:523131.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 15
go:523131.question:
Which of the following can be recurrence relation(s) corresponding to an algorithm with time complexity $\Theta(n)$?

  1. $T(n)=T(n-1)+1, \quad T(1)=1$
  2. $T(n)=2 T\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+1, \quad T(1)=1$
  3. $T(n)=2 T\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+n, \quad T(1)=1$
  4. $T(n)=T(n-1)+n, \quad T(1)=1$

detailed_solution.markdown: Solve each recurrence and compare to $\Theta(n)$: - $T(n)=T(n-1)+1$: unrolling gives $T(n)=T(1)+(n-1)\times1=\Theta(n)$. Matches. - $T(n)=2T(n/2)+1$: by the Master theorem, $a=2,b=2$ so $n^{\log_2 2}=n^1=n$; since $f(n)=1$ is polynomially smaller than $n$, Case 1 gives $T(n)=\Theta(n)$. Matches. - $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n$: this is the classic merge-sort recurrence, $f(n)=n=n^{\log_2 2}$ exactly (Case 2), giving $T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)$ — not $\Theta(n)$. - $T(n)=T(n-1)+n$: unrolling gives $T(n)=\Theta(1+2+\cdots+n)=\Theta(n^2)$ — not $\Theta(n)$.

go:523130.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 16
go:523130.question:
Let $R$ be a binary relation on the set $\{1,2, \ldots, 10\}$, where $(x, y) \in R$ if the product of $x$ and $y$ is square of an integer. Which of the following properties is/are satisfied by $R$?

  1. Reflexive
  2. Symmetric
  3. Transitive
  4. Antisymmetric

detailed_solution.markdown: $(x,y)\in R$ iff $xy$ is a perfect square. - Reflexive: $x\cdot x=x^2$ is always a perfect square, so $(x,x)\in R$ for every $x$. Holds. - Symmetric: $xy=yx$, so if $xy$ is a perfect square then so is $yx$ (the same number). Holds. - Transitive: Write each number as $n=k^2\cdot s$ where $s$ is its square-free part. Then $xy$ is a perfect square exactly when $x$ and $y$ have the same square-free part. This "same square-free part" relation is a genuine equivalence relation, so it is transitive: if $x,y$ share a square-free part and $y,z$ share the same square-free part, then $x,z$ do too, making $xz$ a perfect square. Holds. - Antisymmetric: a counterexample: $x=2,y=8$ gives $xy=16=4^2$, so $(2,8)\in R$ and (by symmetry) $(8,2)\in R$ too, even though $2\ne8$. Fails.

go:523129.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 17
go:523129.question:
For a real number $a$, let $I(a)=\int_{-1}^{1}\left(3 x^{2}-a x+1\right) d x$. Which of the following statements is/are true?

  1. The value of $I(a)$ is independent of the value of $a$
  2. The value of $I(a)$ can vary with the value of $a$
  3. There exists $a \in(-\infty,+\infty)$ such that $I(a)$ is a positive real number
  4. There exists $a \in(-\infty,+\infty)$ such that $I(a)$ is a negative real number

detailed_solution.markdown: $$I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}(3x^2-ax+1)\,dx$$ The middle term $-ax$ is an odd function of $x$, so its integral over the symmetric interval $[-1,1]$ is exactly $0$, regardless of the value of $a$. Only the even part survives: $$I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1(3x^2+1)\,dx=\Big[x^3+x\Big]_{-1}^{1}=(1+1)-(-1-1)=2-(-2)=4$$ So $I(a)=4$ for every real $a$ — the value is completely independent of $a$. Since it's always $4>0$, there certainly exists (in fact, every) $a$ for which $I(a)$ is a positive real number; but there is no $a$ making it negative, and the value does not "vary."

go:523128.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 18
go:523128.question:
In a system, numbers are represented using $4$-bit two's complement form. Consider four numbers $N 1=1011, N 2=1101, N 3=1010$ and $N 4=1001$ in the system. Which of the following operations will result in arithmetic overflow?

  1. $N 1+N 2$
  2. $N 2+N 3$
  3. $N 3-N 4$
  4. $N 1+N 4$

detailed_solution.markdown: Convert each 4-bit two's-complement number to its signed decimal value (invert bits and add $1$ if the leading bit is $1$): $N1{=}1011\to-5,\ N2{=}1101\to-3,\ N3{=}1010\to-6,\ N4{=}1001\to-7$. The representable range for $4$-bit two's complement is $[-8,7]$; a result falling outside this range signals overflow. - $N1+N2=-5+(-3)=-8$ → within range. No overflow. - $N2+N3=-3+(-6)=-9$ → below $-8$. Overflow. - $N3-N4=-6-(-7)=1$ → within range. No overflow. - $N1+N4=-5+(-7)=-12$ → below $-8$. Overflow.

go:523127.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 19
go:523127.question:
Which of the following grammars is/are ambiguous?

  1. $S \rightarrow a S b \mid \epsilon$
  2. $E \rightarrow E+E|E * E| i d$
  3. $S \rightarrow a S|S a| \epsilon$
  4. $S \rightarrow a S \mid \epsilon$

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each grammar for ambiguity (does some string have two distinct parse trees?): - $S\rightarrow aSb\mid\epsilon$: generates only $a^nb^n$, with a unique nested derivation for every string — unambiguous. - $E\rightarrow E+E\mid E*E\mid id$: the classic textbook example of an ambiguous grammar — e.g. $id+id*id$ can be parsed with two different groupings (no precedence/associativity is encoded), giving two distinct parse trees. - $S\rightarrow aS\mid Sa\mid\epsilon$: generates strings of $a$'s only, but because both left-recursion ($Sa$) and right-recursion ($aS$) are available, a string like "$aa$" can be built in more than one structurally distinct way — ambiguous. - $S\rightarrow aS\mid\epsilon$: purely right-recursive, unique derivation for every string — unambiguous.

go:523126.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 20
go:523126.question: The keys $5,28,19,15,26,33,12,17,10$ are inserted into a hash table using the hash function $h(k)=k \bmod 9$. The collisions are resolved by chaining. After all the keys are inserted, the length of the longest chain is $\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown:
Compute $h(k)=k\bmod9$ for each key, then group into chains:

$$\begin{array}{c|c}k&h(k)\\\hline5&5\\28&1\\19&1\\15&6\\26&8\\33&6\\12&3\\17&8\\10&1\end{array}$$

Chains: bucket $1$: $28,19,10$ (length $3$); bucket $6$: $15,33$ (length $2$); bucket $8$: $26,17$ (length $2$); bucket $3$: $12$ (length $1$); bucket $5$: $5$ (length $1$).

The longest chain has length $3$ (bucket $1$, holding $28,19,10$).

go:523125.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 21
go:523125.question:
Consider the system of linear equations given below.
\[
\begin{array}{c}
a x+y=b \\
16 x+a y=24
\end{array}
\]
Suppose the values of $a$ and $b$ are chosen such that the system of linear equations produce multiple solutions. Then the product of $a$ and $b$ is $\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: The system $ax+y=b,\ 16x+ay=24$ has infinitely many (multiple) solutions exactly when the two equations describe the same line, i.e. all three coefficient ratios are equal: $\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}$ From $\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}$: $a^2=16\Rightarrow a=\pm4$. From $\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}$: $b=\dfrac{24}{a}$. If $a=4$: $b=24/4=6$, so $ab=4\times6=24$. If $a=-4$: $b=24/(-4)=-6$, so $ab=(-4)\times(-6)=24$. Either valid choice of $a$ gives the same product.

go:523124.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 22
go:523124.question:
Consider an array $A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31]$. Suppose the merge sort algorithm is executed on array $A$ to sort it in increasing order. The merge sort algorithm will carry out a total of $7$ merge operations.

A merge operation on sorted left array $L$ and sorted right array $R$ is said to be void if the output of the merge operation is the elements of array $L$ followed by the elements of array $R$.

The number of void merge operations among these $7$ merge operations is $\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: A merge is void when every element of the left sub-array is already $\le$ every element of the right sub-array, so the merge simply concatenates them with no interleaving. Trace merge sort on $A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31]$: Bottom level (pairs): $[10],[7]\to[7,10]$ (result is $R$ then $L$, not "$L$ then $R$") — not void. $[8],[19]\to[8,19]$ (already $L$ then $R$ as-is) — void. $[41],[35]\to[35,41]$ — not void. $[25],[31]\to[25,31]$ (already in order) — void. Next level (quads): $[7,10]+[8,19]\to[7,8,10,19]$ (interleaved, not simply $L$ then $R$) — not void. $[35,41]+[25,31]\to[25,31,35,41]$ (interleaved) — not void. Final merge: $[7,8,10,19]+[25,31,35,41]$: every element of the left ($\le19$) is already smaller than every element of the right ($\ge25$), so the merge is simply $L$ followed by $R$ — void. Total merges $=4+2+1=7$ (matches the given count), with exactly $3$ of them void.

go:523123.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 23
go:523123.question: If an IP network uses a subnet mask of $255.255.240.0$, the maximum number of IP addresses that can be assigned to network interfaces is $\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown:
Subnet mask $255.255.240.0$ in binary: $11111111.11111111.11110000.00000000$ — this has $20$ network bits (a $/20$).

Host bits $=32-20=12$, giving $2^{12}=4096$ total addresses in the subnet. Of these, $2$ are reserved (the all-zeros network address and the all-ones broadcast address) and cannot be assigned to interfaces.

Usable addresses $=4096-2=4094$.
