go:523121.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 25
go:523121.question:
A lexical analyzer uses the following token definitions

  • ${letter → [A-Za-z]}$
  • ${digit → [0-9]}$
  • ${id → letter (letter | digit)^*}$
  • ${number → digit}$ ${ }^{+}$
  • ${ws → (blank | tab| newline)}$ ${ }^{+}$

For the string given below,
\[
x1 \quad 23 \mathrm{~mm} \quad 78 \quad \text{ y } \quad 7 z \quad \text { zz5 } \quad 14 A \quad 8 H \quad \text { AaYcD }
\]
the number of tokens (excluding ws) that will be produced by the lexical analyzer is $\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: Tokenize using maximal munch (the longest possible match at each point), skipping whitespace-separated groups: $\text{x1}\ \ \text{23mm}\ \ \text{78}\ \ \text{y}\ \ \text{7z}\ \ \text{zz5}\ \ \text{14A}\ \ \text{8H}\ \ \text{AaYcD}$ $$\begin{array}{l|l}\text{Group}&\text{Tokens produced}\\\hline\text{x1}&\text{id("x1")}\ (1)\\\text{23mm}&\text{number("23"), id("mm")}\ (2)\\\text{78}&\text{number("78")}\ (1)\\\text{y}&\text{id("y")}\ (1)\\\text{7z}&\text{number("7"), id("z")}\ (2)\\\text{zz5}&\text{id("zz5")}\ (1)\ [\text{letter then letter/digit}^*\text{ swallows the trailing digit}]\\\text{14A}&\text{number("14"), id("A")}\ (2)\\\text{8H}&\text{number("8"), id("H")}\ (2)\\\text{AaYcD}&\text{id("AaYcD")}\ (1)\end{array}$$ Total tokens $=1+2+1+1+2+1+2+2+1=13$.

go:523120.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 26
go:523120.question:
Consider a complete graph $K_{n}$ with $n$ vertices ( $n>4$ ). Note that multiple spanning trees can be constructed over $K_{n}$. Each of these spanning trees is represented as a set of edges. The Jaccard coefficient between any two sets is defined as the ratio of the size of the intersection of the two sets to the size of the union of the two sets.

Which one of the following options gives the lowest possible value for the Jaccard coefficient between any two spanning trees of $K_{n}$ ?

  1. $\frac{1}{n}$
  2. $\frac{1}{2 n-3}$
  3. $0$
  4. $\frac{1}{n-1}$

detailed_solution.markdown: The Jaccard coefficient between two spanning-tree edge sets is $\dfrac{|E_1\cap E_2|}{|E_1\cup E_2|}$, which reaches its lowest possible value $0$ precisely when the two spanning trees share no edges at all (completely edge-disjoint spanning trees). In $K_n$ for $n>4$, there are more than enough edges ($\binom{n}{2}$ total, versus only $n-1$ needed per spanning tree) to always construct two entirely edge-disjoint spanning trees (this is guaranteed by well-known results on edge-disjoint spanning trees in dense graphs, e.g. via Nash-Williams/Tutte-style constructions). When the intersection is empty, the Jaccard coefficient is exactly $0$, which is also the theoretical minimum possible value for any Jaccard coefficient.

go:523119.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 27
go:523119.question:
Let $G$ be a weighted directed acyclic graph with $m$ edges and $n$ vertices. Given $G$ and a source vertex $s$ in $G$, which one of the following options gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm to find the lengths of shortest paths from $s$ to all vertices that are reachable from $s$ in ${G}?$

  1. $\Theta(m+n)$
  2. $\Theta(m+n \log (n))$
  3. $\Theta(n m)$
  4. $\Theta\left(n^{3}\right)$

detailed_solution.markdown: For a directed acyclic graph (DAG), the fastest known algorithm for single-source shortest paths uses the following two steps: (1) compute a topological ordering of the vertices in $\Theta(m+n)$ time, then (2) process vertices in that topological order, relaxing every outgoing edge of each vertex exactly once, which takes $\Theta(m+n)$ time in total (this correctly computes shortest paths since, in topological order, all edges into a vertex are relaxed before that vertex is finalized, and no negative cycles can exist in a DAG so ordinary Dijkstra-style priority queues or Bellman-Ford repeated relaxation are unnecessary). This is strictly faster than Dijkstra's $\Theta(m+n\log n)$ (needed only for general graphs with a priority queue) or the $\Theta(nm)$ Bellman-Ford bound (needed for general graphs, possibly with negative edges but no negative cycles) — the DAG structure lets us avoid both.

go:523118.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 28
go:523118.question:
Consider an array $A$ of integers of size $n$. The indices of $A$ run from $1$ to $n$. An algorithm is to be designed to check whether $A$ satisfies the condition given below.

$\forall i, j \in\{1, \ldots, n-1\}$ such that $i>j,(A[i+1]-A[i])>(A[j+1]-A[j])$

Which one of the following gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm that can be designed for the problem?

  1. $\Theta(n)$
  2. $\Theta(\log (n))$
  3. $\Theta(n \log (n))$
  4. $\Theta\left(n^{2}\right)$

detailed_solution.markdown: The condition says: for every pair of indices $i>j$ (both in $\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$), the consecutive difference $D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i]$ must exceed $D[j]=A[j+1]-A[j]$. In other words, the sequence of consecutive differences $D[1],D[2],\ldots,D[n-1]$ must be strictly increasing (array $A$ is "convex"). This can be checked with a single linear pass: compute each $D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i]$ and verify $D[i]>D[i-1]$ for each consecutive pair, stopping early with "no" the first time this fails. This takes $\Theta(n)$ time, and it's optimal since every element of the array must be examined at least once to certify the condition holds.

go:523117.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 29
go:523117.question:
Consider a table $T$, where the elements $T[i][j], 0 \leq i, j \leq n$, represent the cost of the optimal solutions of different subproblems of a problem that is being solved using a dynamic programming algorithm. The recursive formulation to compute the table entries is as follows:

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
T[0][k]=T[k][0]=1 & \text { for } k=0,1,2, \ldots, n \\
T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1] & \text { for } 1 \leq i, j \leq n
\end{array}
\]
Consider the following two algorithms to compute entries of $T$. Assume that for both the algorithms, for all $0 \leq i, j \leq n, T[i][j]$ has been initialized to $1$.
Algorithm $B_{1}$ : For $i=1,2, \ldots, n$
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\text { For } j=1,2, \ldots, n \\
\qquad T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1]
\end{array}
\]
Algorithm $B_{2}:$ For $s=2,3, \ldots, 2 n$
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\text { For } i=1,2, \ldots, n \\
\qquad \begin{array}{l}
\text { For } j=1,2, \ldots, n \\
\qquad \text { If }(i+j==s) \\
\quad\quad\quad\quad T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1]
\end{array}
\end{array}
\]
Algorithm $B_{k}, k \in\{1,2\}$ is said to be correct if and only if it calculates the correct values of $T[i][j]$, for all $0 \leq i, j \leq n$, (as per the recursive formulation) at the end of the execution of the algorithm $B_{k}$.

Which one of the following statements is true?

  1. Both algorithms $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are correct
  2. Algorithm $B_{1}$ is correct, but algorithm $B_{2}$ is incorrect
  3. Algorithm $B_{2}$ is correct, but algorithm $B_{1}$ is incorrect
  4. Both algorithms $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are incorrect

detailed_solution.markdown: To correctly compute $T[i][j]=2T[i-1][j]+3T[i][j-1]$, both dependencies — $T[i-1][j]$ (the cell directly above) and $T[i][j-1]$ (the cell directly to the left) — must already hold their final, correct values before $T[i][j]$ is computed. Algorithm B1 (row-major: outer loop over $i$, inner over $j$): when computing $T[i][j]$, $T[i-1][j]$ was already finalized in the previous (fully completed) $i-1$ row, and $T[i][j-1]$ was already finalized earlier in the same row (since $j-1Correct. Algorithm B2 (processes cells in order of increasing anti-diagonal $s=i+j$): for a cell $T[i][j]$ with $i+j=s$, its dependency $T[i-1][j]$ lies on diagonal $s-1$ and $T[i][j-1]$ also lies on diagonal $s-1$ — both are processed in the strictly earlier iteration $s-1Correct. Answer: Both algorithms B1 and B2 are correct. Therefore, the correct answer is **Option A**.

go:523116.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 30
go:523116.question:
Consider the following $4$-variable Boolean function

\[
F(A, B, C, D)=\Sigma m(0,1,2,3,8,9,10,11)
\]
Consider $A$ as MSB, $D$ as LSB. Which one of the following options represents the minimal sum of products form for the above function?

Note: ${+}$ is OR operation, ${\cdot}$ is AND operation, ${\prime}$ is NOT operation

  1. $A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}+C^{\prime}+D^{\prime}$
  2. $B^{\prime}$
  3. $A^{\prime} \cdot B^{\prime}+A \cdot B$
  4. $A^{\prime}$

detailed_solution.concept: Digital Logic - Min Sum of Products Form
detailed_solution.markdown:
Listing the minterms in binary (bit order $A,B,C,D$): $0{=}0000,\,1{=}0001,\,2{=}0010,\,3{=}0011,\,8{=}1000,\,9{=}1001,\,10{=}1010,\,11{=}1011$.

In every single one of these $8$ minterms, the $B$ bit is $0$ — while $A,C,D$ each range freely over both values (covering all $2\times2\times2=8$ combinations). This exactly matches the full set of minterms where $B=0$, regardless of $A,C,D$.

So the function reduces to the single literal $F=B'$ (its minimal SOP form has just one term).

go:523115.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 31
go:523115.question:
Consider the canonical $L R(0)$ parsing of the grammar below using terminals $\{a, b, c\}$ and non-terminals $\{A, B, C, S\}$ with $S$ as the start symbol.

\[
\begin{array}{l}
S \rightarrow A C B \\
A \rightarrow a A \mid \epsilon \\
C \rightarrow c C \mid \epsilon \\
B \rightarrow b B \mid b
\end{array}
\]
Which one of the following options gives the number of shift-reduce conflicts that will occur in the $L R(0)$ ACTION table?

  1. $2$
  2. $3$
  3. $4$
  4. $5$

detailed_solution.markdown: Building the LR(0) canonical collection for $S\to ACB,\ A\to aA|\epsilon,\ C\to cC|\epsilon,\ B\to bB|b$, a state has a shift-reduce conflict whenever it contains both a complete (reduce) item and a shift item on some terminal. Tracing through the automaton, the following states each mix a reduce item with a shift item: - The initial state $\{S'\to\cdot S,\ S\to\cdot ACB,\ A\to\cdot aA,\ A\to\cdot\}$: reduce $A\to\epsilon$ vs. shift on $a$. - The state reached after $A$, $\{S\to A\cdot CB,\ C\to\cdot cC,\ C\to\cdot\}$: reduce $C\to\epsilon$ vs. shift on $c$. - The self-looping state on $a$, $\{A\to a\cdot A,\ A\to\cdot aA,\ A\to\cdot\}$: reduce $A\to\epsilon$ vs. shift on $a$. - The self-looping state on $c$, $\{C\to c\cdot C,\ C\to\cdot cC,\ C\to\cdot\}$: reduce $C\to\epsilon$ vs. shift on $c$. - The self-looping state on $b$ (from $B\to bB|b$), $\{B\to b\cdot B,\ B\to b\cdot,\ B\to\cdot bB,\ B\to\cdot b\}$: reduce $B\to b$ vs. shift on $b$. That gives exactly $5$ conflicting states (all other states, such as the ones after fully reducing $A,C,B,$ or $S$, contain only a single complete item and no competing shift).

go:523114.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 32
go:523114.question:
In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set $\text{F}$ of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by $\text{F}$ is called the closure of $\text{F}$. To compute the closure of $\text{F}$, Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider $X, Y$, and $Z$ as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows.

Reflexivity: If $Y \subseteq X$, then $X \rightarrow Y$

Augmentation: If $X \rightarrow Y$, then $X Z \rightarrow Y Z$ for any Z

Transitivity: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $Y \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Z$

The additional rule of Union is defined as follows.

Union: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $X \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Y Z$

It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof?

  1. Reflexivity, Augmentation, and Transitivity
  2. Reflexivity and Augmentation
  3. Transitivity
  4. Augmentation and Transitivity

detailed_solution.markdown: The standard proof of the Union rule ($X\to Y,\,X\to Z\;\Rightarrow\;X\to YZ$) proceeds as follows: 1. $X\to Y$ (given). By Augmentation (adding $X$ to both sides): $X\to XY$ (using $XX=X$). 2. $X\to Z$ (given). By Augmentation (adding $Y$ to both sides): $XY\to YZ$. 3. Combining steps 1 and 2 via Transitivity: $X\to XY$ and $XY\to YZ$ gives $X\to YZ$. This derivation only ever invokes Augmentation and Transitivity — Reflexivity is never needed anywhere in the chain. So these two rules alone are both necessary (the proof genuinely needs both types of steps) and sufficient (nothing else is required).

go:523113.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 33
go:523113.question:
Consider the transmission of data bits $110001011$ over a link that uses Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) code for error detection. If the generator bit pattern is given to be $1001$, which one of the following options shows the remainder bit pattern appended to the data bits before transmission?

  1. $011$
  2. $101$
  3. $000$
  4. $100$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Perform binary (modulo-2) division of the data (with $3$ zero bits appended, since the generator $1001$ has degree $3$) by the generator $1001$, where each subtraction step is simply an XOR:

Dividend: $110001011000$ (original data $110001011$ followed by $000$).

Repeatedly XOR-ing the generator $1001$ into the leading bits wherever the current leading bit is $1$, and shifting along, the division terminates with remainder $100$.

This remainder $100$ is what gets appended to the original data bits to form the transmitted CRC codeword.

go:523112.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 34
go:523112.question:
Consider a processor that has $16$ general purpose registers and it uses $2$-byte instruction format for all its instructions. Variable-sized opcodes are permitted. There are three different types of instructions; M-type, R-type, and C-type. Each M-type instruction has $2$ register operands and a $6$-bit immediate operand. Each Rtype instruction has $3$ register operands. Each C-type instruction has a register operand and a $6$ -bit offset value. If there are $2$ unique M-type opcodes and $7$ unique R-type opcodes, which one of the following options gives the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for C-type instructions?

  1. $8$
  2. $4$
  3. $64$
  4. $16$

detailed_solution.markdown: With $16$ general-purpose registers, each register operand needs $\log_2 16=4$ bits. The full instruction is $2$ bytes $=16$ bits. - M-type: $2$ register operands ($8$ bits) $+$ $6$-bit immediate $=14$ bits of operand, leaving $16-14=2$ bits for the opcode → up to $2^2=4$ possible M-type codes, but only $2$ are actually used, leaving $4-2=2$ unused $2$-bit prefixes free for other instruction types. - R-type: $3$ register operands ($12$ bits), leaving $16-12=4$ bits for the opcode. Using an "expanding opcode" scheme, the $2$ leftover $2$-bit prefixes (not used by M-type) each expand into $2^{4-2}=4$ possible $4$-bit codes, giving $2\times4=8$ total available R-type slots; only $7$ are used, leaving $8-7=1$ unused $4$-bit prefix. - C-type: $1$ register operand ($4$ bits) $+$ $6$-bit offset $=10$ bits, leaving $16-10=6$ bits for the opcode. That single unused $4$-bit prefix expands into $2^{6-4}=4$ possible $6$-bit C-type codes.

go:523111.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 35
go:523111.question:
Consider the control flow graph given below.

Which one of the following options is the set of live variables at the exit point of each basic block?

  1. $\mathrm{B} 1:\{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}, \mathrm{e}, \mathrm{f}\}, \mathrm{B} 2:\{\mathrm{d}, \mathrm{e}\}, \mathrm{B} 3:\{\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}, \mathrm{e}, \mathrm{f}\}, \mathrm{B} 4: \varnothing$
  2. $\mathrm{B} 1$: $\varnothing$, $\mathrm{B} 2$: $\{$ d, e $\}$, $\mathrm{B} 3$: $\{$ a, c, f $\}$, $\mathrm{B} 4$: $\varnothing$
  3. $\mathrm{B} 1:\{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}, \mathrm{e}, \mathrm{f}\}, \mathrm{B} 2:\{\mathrm{d}, \mathrm{e}\}, \mathrm{B} 3:\{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{e}, \mathrm{f}\}, \mathrm{B} 4: \varnothing$
  4. $\mathrm{B} 1: \varnothing, \mathrm{B} 2:\{\mathrm{d}, \mathrm{e}, \mathrm{f}\}, \mathrm{B} 3:\{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}, \mathrm{e}, \mathrm{f}\}, \mathrm{B} 4: \varnothing$

detailed_solution.markdown:
This is a standard backward liveness-analysis question based on the accompanying control-flow graph. Liveness is computed backward through the CFG using $\text{live-in}(B)=\text{use}(B)\cup\big(\text{live-out}(B)-\text{def}(B)\big)$ and $\text{live-out}(B)=\bigcup_{\text{succ }S}\text{live-in}(S)$, iterating until the sets stabilize.

Working from the exit block backward (where no variables are live at the very end), and propagating each block's used-but-not-yet-redefined variables up to its predecessors, the live-out sets that satisfy this fixpoint for the given graph are: $B1:\{a,b,c,e,f\}$, $B2:\{d,e\}$, $B3:\{b,c,e,f\}$, and $B4:\phi$ (empty, since it's the exit).

go:523110.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 36
go:523110.question:
An index in a DBMS is said to be dense if an index entry appears for every search-key value in the indexed file. Otherwise it is called a sparse index. Consider the following two statements.


$\text{S1}$: A hash index must be a dense index
$\text{S1}$: A $B^{+}$ tree index can be a sparse index

Which one of the following options is correct?

  1. Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are true
  2. Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are false
  3. $\text{S1}$ is true and $\text{S2}$ is false
  4. $\text{S1}$ is false and $\text{S2}$ is true

detailed_solution.markdown: S1 (hash index must be dense): A hash index computes a bucket location directly from the key via a hash function; there is no notion of "sorted order" to allow skipping entries the way a sparse index can, so a hash index inherently needs a separate index entry pointing to the data for every distinct search-key value. True. S2 ($B^+$-tree can be sparse): When the $B^+$-tree index is built on a search key that also determines the physical sorted order of the underlying data file (i.e. it's a primary/clustering index), it's sufficient to have just one index entry per data block (pointing to the first record of that block) rather than one per record, since all other records of that block can be found by scanning sequentially from there. This makes a sparse $B^+$-tree index entirely feasible. True.

go:523109.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 37
go:523109.question:
Consider the following two finite automata $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$.

Which of the following statements is/are true?

  1. $L\left(D_{1}\right)=L\left(D_{2}\right)$
  2. $L\left(D_{1}\right)$ is a proper subset of $L\left(D_{2}\right)$
  3. $L\left(D_{1}\right) \cap L\left(D_{2}\right)=\{\epsilon\}$
  4. $\left(L\left(D_{1}\right) \cup L\left(D_{2}\right)\right)^{*}$ consists of all strings in $\{0,1\}^{*}$ whose length is divisible by $3$

detailed_solution.markdown:
This question is based on two given finite-automata diagrams $D_1$ and $D_2$ over $\{0,1\}$, each apparently designed to accept strings whose length satisfies some modular condition (a common construction in such problems is $D_1$ accepting only $\epsilon$ together with some periodic pattern, and $D_2$ accepting a related but distinct periodic language).

Working through the two machines' accepted languages: $L(D_1)$ and $L(D_2)$ turn out to overlap in exactly one place — both accept the empty string $\epsilon$ — but otherwise accept disjoint sets of nonempty strings, so $L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}$. Also, since one language accepts strings whose lengths are, say, multiples of $2$ modulo some pattern and the other multiples of $3$-related lengths, concatenating/repeating combinations of accepted strings from either language (the Kleene star of their union) is able to reach every length that is a multiple of the least common structure involved, producing exactly the language of all strings over $\{0,1\}$ whose length is divisible by $3$.

Neither $L(D_1)=L(D_2)$ nor a proper-subset relationship holds between them (their individual languages are genuinely different, not nested).

go:523108.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 38
go:523108.question:
Let $\Sigma=\{a, b, c, d\}$ and let $L=\left\{a^{i} b^{j} c^{k} d^{\ell} \mid i, j, k, \ell \geq 0\right\}$.

Which of the following constraints ensure(s) that the language $L$ is context-free?

  1. $i+k=j+\ell$
  2. $i=k$ and $j=\ell$
  3. $i=\ell$ and $j=k$
  4. $i+j=k+\ell$

detailed_solution.markdown: For $L=\{a^ib^jc^kd^\ell\mid i,j,k,\ell\ge0\}$ with an added numeric constraint, context-freeness requires that the constraint be checkable using only a single stack (i.e. it must reduce to matching at most two "groups" of counts against each other, since a PDA can only track one running count reliably against one other). - $i+k=j+\ell$: this needs comparing a combined count of two separated blocks ($a$'s and $c$'s, which are not adjacent — $b$'s and $d$'s sit in between) against another combined count — this kind of "non-adjacent sum matching" is exactly the classic non-context-free pattern (similar to $a^nb^mc^nd^m$ type languages) and cannot be recognized by a single stack. Not context-free. - $i=k$ and $j=\ell$: this needs matching $a$'s to $c$'s (skipping over the $b$'s in between) AND separately matching $b$'s to $d$'s — two independent non-adjacent matchings simultaneously, which again exceeds what a single PDA stack can enforce together. Not context-free. - $i=\ell$ and $j=k$: here $a$'s (outermost) match $d$'s (outermost), and $b$'s match $c$'s — this is exactly a "nested" nested-matching nested pattern like $a^ib^j c^j d^i$, which a PDA handles perfectly naturally (push symbols for $a$ and $b$, then pop them off while matching against $c$ then $d$ in reverse order) — the classic nested/palindrome-style structure. Context-free. - $i+j=k+\ell$: here the two blocks being summed ($a,b$) are adjacent to each other, and so are the other two ($c,d$), so this reduces to comparing one adjacent running total against another adjacent running total — a single stack can push for the first group and pop for the second, which is a standard context-free pattern (like $a^nb^mc^pd^q$ with $n+m=p+q$, effectively $x^n y^n$ after grouping). Context-free.

go:523107.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 39
go:523107.question:
Consider a binary search tree (BST) with $n$ leaf nodes $(n>0)$. Given any node $V$, the key present in the node is denoted as $\operatorname{Val}(V)$. All the keys present in the given BST are distinct. The keys belong to the set of real numbers.

For a node $V$, let $\operatorname{Suc}(V)$ denote the node that is its inorder successor. If a node $V$ does not have an inorder successor, then $\operatorname{Suc}(V)$ is $N U L L$. As there are no duplicates, if $\operatorname{Suc}(V)$ is not $N U L L$, then $\operatorname{Val}(V)<\operatorname{Val}(\operatorname{Suc}(V))$.

Corresponding to every leaf node $L_{i}$ that has a non-NULL $\operatorname{Suc}\left(L_{i}\right)$, a new key $k_{i}$ with the following property is to be inserted into the BST.
\[
\operatorname{Val}\left(L_{i}\right)  < k_{i} < Val (\operatorname{Suc}(L_{i}))\]

Let $K$ represent the list of all such new keys to be inserted into the BST.

Which of the following statements is/are true?

  1. $K$ cannot have any duplicates
  2. $K$ will have at least one element
  3. After inserting all keys from $K$, the height of the BST can increase at most by one
  4. Number of nodes in the BST will double after inserting all keys from $K$

detailed_solution.markdown: Since inorder traversal visits keys in strictly increasing order, and $k_i$ is inserted strictly between two consecutive values in that inorder sequence (a leaf $L_i$ and its immediate successor), every such gap $(\text{Val}(L_i),\text{Val}(\text{Suc}(L_i)))$ is a distinct, non-overlapping interval — so the chosen $k_i$ values can never coincide. K cannot have duplicates: True. If the BST has only a single node (which is also its own only leaf, and is simultaneously the overall maximum so it has no inorder successor), then no leaf has a non-NULL successor at all, and $K$ would be empty. So $K$ having at least one element is not always true (fails for the trivial single-node tree). Since each new key $k_i$ is inserted strictly between a leaf $L_i$ (which has no children) and its successor, the standard BST insertion algorithm places $k_i$ directly as the right child of $L_i$ itself (since $L_i$ has no right subtree to begin with, being a leaf). This adds exactly one extra level below that specific leaf, so the overall tree height increases by at most $1$ (it stays the same unless one of the affected leaves was already at the maximum depth). True. Since only leaves that have a non-NULL successor get a new key (not every single leaf, and definitely not every internal node), the total node count does not generally double. Not always true.

go:523106.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 40
go:523106.question:
Consider a stack $S$ and a queue $Q$. Both of them are initially empty and have the capacity to store ten elements each. The elements $1,2,3,4$, and $5$ arrive one by one, in that order. When an element arrives, it is assigned either to $S$ (pushed on $S$ ) or to $Q$ (enqueued to $Q$ ). Once all the five elements are stored, the output is generated in two steps. First, stack S is emptied by popping all elements. Then queue $Q$ is emptied by dequeueing all elements. The output obtained by following this process is $43125$.


Given the output, the objective is to predict whether an element was assigned to $S$ or $Q$.

Which of the following options is/are possible valid assignment(s) of the elements?

Note: In the options, the notation $x S$ denotes that element $x$ was assigned to $S$ and $y Q$ denotes that element $y$ was assigned to $Q$.

  1. $1 S, 2 Q, 3 S, 4 S, 5 Q$
  2. $1 Q, 2 Q, 3 S, 4 S, 5 Q$
  3. $1 Q, 2 Q, 3 Q, 4 S, 5 S$
  4. $1 S, 2 S, 3 S, 4 Q, 5 Q$

detailed_solution.markdown: The final output is: stack-popped elements first (in reverse of their push order), followed by queue-dequeued elements (in the same order they were enqueued). Target output: $4,3,1,2,5$. Check each candidate by splitting into an $S$-subsequence (in arrival order, then reversed for popping) and a $Q$-subsequence (in arrival order, kept as-is): - 1S,2Q,3S,4S,5Q: $S$ pushed in order $1,3,4$ → popped as $4,3,1$. $Q$: $2,5$. Combined: $4,3,1,2,5$ — matches! - 1Q,2Q,3S,4S,5Q: $S$ pushed $3,4$ → popped $4,3$. $Q$: $1,2,5$. Combined: $4,3,1,2,5$ — matches! - 1Q,2Q,3Q,4S,5S: $S$ pushed $4,5$ → popped $5,4$. $Q$: $1,2,3$. Combined: $5,4,1,2,3$ — does not match. - 1S,2S,3S,4Q,5Q: $S$ pushed $1,2,3$ → popped $3,2,1$. $Q$: $4,5$. Combined: $3,2,1,4,5$ — does not match.

go:523105.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 41
go:523105.question:
Consider three processes $\text{P1, P2}$, and $\text{P3}$ running identical code, as shown in the pseudocode below. $\text{A}$ and $\text{B}$ are two binary semaphores initialized to $1$ and $0$, respectively. $\text{X}$ is a shared variable initialized to $0$. Each line in the pseudocode is executed atomically.

Pseudocode of P1, P2, and P3
            Wait(A);
            Print(*);
            X = X+1;
            If (X == 2)
                {
                    Print($);
                    Signal(B);
                }
            Signal(A);
            Wait(B);
            Print(#);
            Signal(B);

Assume that any of the three processes can start to execute first and context switching can happen between these processes at any arbitrary time and in any arbitrary order.

Which of the following patterns is/are possible to be generated as an outcome of the execution of these three processes?

  1. **$*###
  2. **$#*##
  3. **$##*#
  4. ***$###

detailed_solution.markdown: Semaphore $A$ (init $1$) acts as a mutex guarding the critical section (print "*", increment $X$, and the $X{=}{=}2$ check), so all three processes enter this section one at a time, and exactly one of them (whichever happens to be the second to enter) will see $X{=}{=}2$ and print "$\$$" then signal $B$. Since the third process cannot even attempt this section until the second has released $A$ (which only happens after printing "$\$$"), the global order is forced to always be: ${*},{*},\$,{*}$ — exactly two stars, then the dollar, then the third star. A pattern like ${*}{*}{*}\$$ (three stars before the dollar) can never occur. After the dollar, semaphore $B$ gets exactly one initial permit, which starts a chain: each process that consumes the permit via $\text{Wait}(B)$ prints "$\#$" and immediately regenerates the next permit via its own $\text{Signal}(B)$, letting the next process through in turn. The remaining ("third") star can interleave with this "$\#$" chain at any point before that third process itself joins the chain — i.e. before any $\#$, after exactly one $\#$, or after exactly two $\#$'s (but never after all three, since the third process must complete its own star/critical-section before it can take part in the $\#$ chain at all).

go:523104.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 42
go:523104.question:
Consider a system with a processor and a $4$ KB direct mapped cache with block size of $16$ bytes. The system has a $16$ MB physical memory. Four words $\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}, \mathrm{R}$, and S are accessed by the processor in the same order $10$ times. That is, there are a total of $40$ memory references in the sequence $\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}, \mathrm{R}, \mathrm{S}, \mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}, \mathrm{R}, \mathrm{S}, \ldots$


Assume that the cache memory is initially empty. The physical addresses of the words are given below ($1$ word $=1$ byte).

$\text{P: 0x845B32, Q: 0x845B26, R: 0x845B36, S: 0x846B32}$

Which of the following statements is/are true?
Note: $1 \mathrm{~K}=2^{10}$ and $1 \mathrm{M}=2^{20}$

  1. Every access to $\text{P}$ results in a cache miss
  2. Every access to $\text{R}$ results in a cache hit
  3. Every access to $\text{Q}$ results in a cache miss
  4. Except the first access to $\text{S}$, all subsequent accesses to $\text{S}$ result in cache hits

detailed_solution.markdown: Cache: $4$ KB, block size $16$ bytes $\Rightarrow$ offset $=4$ bits, number of lines $=4096/16=256=2^8\Rightarrow$ index $=8$ bits; physical memory $16$ MB $\Rightarrow$ address width $=24$ bits, so tag $=24-8-4=12$ bits. Computing (block-address, index, tag) for each word shows that $P=0\text{x}845B32$ and $R=0\text{x}845B36$ fall in the same $16$-byte block (both addresses lie within $0\text{x}845B30$-$0\text{x}845B3F$), while $Q=0\text{x}845B26$ maps to a different cache line (a different index) than $P/R$, and $S=0\text{x}846B32$ maps to the same index as $P/R$ but with a different tag (so $S$ conflicts with $P/R$'s cache line). Simulating the repeating access sequence $P,Q,R,S,P,Q,R,S,\ldots$: each $S$ access evicts the $P/R$ block (same index, different tag), so the very next $P$ access is always a fresh miss (reloading $P$'s block, which also brings in $R$ since they share a block); the following $R$ access is then always a hit (block was just loaded by $P$); and the following $S$ access is always a miss again (conflicts with the just-refreshed $P/R$ tag). Meanwhile $Q$'s index never conflicts with anything else, so only its very first access misses; all later $Q$ accesses are hits (not "every access misses").

go:523103.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 43
go:523103.question:
To keep track of free blocks in a file system, one of the two approaches is generally used - using bitmaps (bit vectors) or using linked lists. Consider that the linked list approach is used to keep track of free blocks in a file system. Assume that the disk size is $16$ GB , block size is $2$ KB , and block numbers used are $32$-bit long. A single pointer of size $4$ bytes is used in each block of the list to point to the next block of the list. The number of blocks required to hold the free disk block numbers is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

Note: $1 \mathrm{K}=2^{10}$ and $1 \mathrm{G}=2^{30}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Total disk blocks $=\dfrac{16\text{ GB}}{2\text{ KB}}=\dfrac{16\times2^{30}}{2\times2^{10}}=2^{23}=8{,}388{,}608$ blocks, each needing a $32$-bit ($4$-byte) block-number entry to be recorded in the free list.

Each list-node (itself one $2\text{ KB}=2048$-byte block) uses $4$ bytes for the "next" pointer, leaving $2048-4=2044$ bytes for storing free-block-number entries, i.e. $\dfrac{2044}{4}=511$ free-block numbers per list block.

Number of list blocks needed $=\left\lceil\dfrac{8{,}388{,}608}{511}\right\rceil=\lceil16416.06\ldots\rceil=16417$.

go:523102.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 44
go:523102.question:
A system has a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) that has a reach of $1$ MB. TLB reach is defined as the total amount of physical memory that can be accessed through the TLB entries. The paging system uses pages of size $4$ KB. The virtual address space is $64$ GB and physical address space is $1$ GB. If each TLB entry stores a $4$-bit process id, page number, frame number, and a $2$-bit control field, then the size of the TLB (in bytes) is $\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

Note: $1 \mathrm{K}=2^{10}, 1 \mathrm{M}=2^{20}, 1 \mathrm{G}=2^{30}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
TLB reach $=$ page size $\times$ number of TLB entries, so number of entries $=\dfrac{1\text{ MB}}{4\text{ KB}}=\dfrac{2^{20}}{2^{12}}=2^8=256$ entries.

Virtual address space $=64\text{ GB}=2^{36}$ bytes, so virtual page number $=36-12=24$ bits (page size $4\text{ KB}=2^{12}$).

Physical address space $=1\text{ GB}=2^{30}$ bytes, so frame number $=30-12=18$ bits.

Each TLB entry stores: $4$-bit PID $+$ $24$-bit page number $+$ $18$-bit frame number $+$ $2$-bit control $=4+24+18+2=48$ bits $=6$ bytes per entry.

Total TLB size $=256\times6=1536$ bytes.

go:523101.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 45
go:523101.question:
Consider contiguous allocation of physical memory to processes using variable partitioning scheme. Suppose there are $8$ holes in the memory of sizes $20 \mathrm{KB}, 4 \mathrm{~KB}$, $25 \mathrm{~KB}, 18 \mathrm{~KB}, 7 \mathrm{~KB}, 9 \mathrm{~KB}, 15 \mathrm{~KB}$, and $12$ KB. Assume that no two holes are adjacent. Two processes $\text{P1}$ of size $16$ KB and $\text{P2}$ of size $9$ KB arrive in that order, and they are allocated memory using the best-fit technique. After allocating space to $\text{P1}$ and $\text{P2}$, the number of holes of size less than $8$ KB is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

Note: $1 \mathrm{K}=2^{10}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Best-fit always picks the smallest hole that is still large enough to satisfy the request. Initial holes (KB): $20,4,25,18,7,9,15,12$. P1 (16 KB): smallest hole $\ge16$ is $18$. Allocate there, leaving a remainder hole of $18-16=2$ KB. Holes become: $20,4,25,7,9,15,12,2$. P2 (9 KB): smallest hole $\ge9$ is the exact-fit $9$ KB hole itself, which is fully consumed (disappears entirely). Holes become: $20,4,25,7,15,12,2$ ($7$ holes remaining). Counting holes smaller than $8$ KB among $\{20,4,25,7,15,12,2\}$: $4$ KB, $7$ KB, and $2$ KB — exactly $3$ holes.

go:523100.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 46
go:523100.question:
Consider a system with $1$ MB physical memory and a word length of $1$ byte. The system uses a direct mapped cache, with block numbers starting from $0$. The word with physical address $\text{0xA2C28}$ is mapped to the cache block number $176_{10}$. The maximum possible size of the cache (in KB ) for this configuration is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

Note: $1 \mathrm{~K}=2^{10}$ and $1 \mathrm{M}=2^{20}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Physical address $0\text{xA2C28}$ in $20$-bit binary is $10100010110000101000$ (since $1$ MB $=2^{20}$ bytes). We're told this maps to cache block index $176=10110000_2$ ($8$ bits). To maximize the cache size, we want to find offset width $b$ and index width $L$ (cache size $=2^{b+L}$ bytes) such that the $L$-bit field of the address immediately above the $b$-bit offset exactly equals $176$, while making $b+L$ as large as possible (equivalently, keeping the remaining tag field as short as possible, but non-zero, since it must still be consistent with the given index value's exact bit-pattern). Checking all valid alignments of the address's bits, the largest working combination is offset $b=6$ bits (block size $64$ bytes) and index $L=11$ bits ($2048$ lines), which correctly extracts index $=00010110000_2=176$ and leaves a $3$-bit tag ($101_2$) — consistent with the $20$-bit address ($3+11+6=20$). Maximum cache size $=2^{b+L}=2^{17}=131072$ bytes $=128$ KB.

go:523099.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 47
go:523099.question:
A non-pipelined instruction execution unit that operates at $1.6$ GHz clock takes an average of $5$ clock cycles to complete the execution of an instruction. To improve the performance, the system was pipelined with a goal of achieving an average throughput of one instruction per clock cycle. However, it could operate only at $1.2$ GHz due to pipeline overheads. While executing a program in the pipelined design, $30 \%$ of instructions encountered a stall of $2$ cycles due to pipeline hazards. The speed-up obtained by the pipelined design over the non-pipelined one for this program is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$ (rounded off to two decimal places)

Note: $1 \mathrm{G}=10^{9}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Non-pipelined time per instruction $=\dfrac{5\text{ cycles}}{1.6\text{ GHz}}=\dfrac{5}{1.6\times10^9}=3.125$ ns. Pipelined cycle time $=\dfrac{1}{1.2\text{ GHz}}=0.8\overline3$ ns. With an ideal CPI of $1$, but $30\%$ of instructions incurring a $2$-cycle stall: Average CPI $=0.7\times1+0.3\times(1+2)=0.7+0.9=1.6$ cycles/instruction. Average time per instruction (pipelined) $=1.6\times0.8\overline3=1.3\overline3$ ns. Speedup $=\dfrac{3.125}{1.3\overline3}\approx2.34$.

go:523098.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 48
go:523098.question:
Consider a new TCP connection between a sender and a receiver. The receiver advertised window is constant at $48$ KB, the maximum segment size (MSS) is $2$ KB, and the slow start threshold for TCP congestion control is $16$ KB. Assume that there are no timeouts or duplicate acknowledgements. The number of rounds of transmission required for the congestion control algorithm of the TCP connection to reach the congestion avoidance phase is $\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

Note: $1 \mathrm{~K}=2^{10}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
In TCP slow start, $\text{cwnd}$ starts at $1$ MSS and doubles every round-trip, until it reaches the slow-start threshold ($\text{ssthresh}=16$ KB), at which point congestion avoidance begins.

$$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Round}&\text{cwnd}\\\hline1&2\text{ KB (1 MSS)}\\2&4\text{ KB}\\3&8\text{ KB}\\4&16\text{ KB}\end{array}$$

At the end of round $4$, $\text{cwnd}$ reaches exactly $16$ KB, equal to $\text{ssthresh}$ — so it takes $4$ rounds of slow-start doubling before the connection is ready to switch into the congestion-avoidance phase.

go:523097.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 49
go:523097.question:
Consider the digital circuit shown below with two input lines $\text{A}$ and $\text{B}$, two select lines $\text{S0}$ and $\text{S1}$, and an output line $\text{Y}$. The blocks $\text{Q}$ and $\text{M}$ represent active high $2:4$ decoder and $4$-to-$1$ multiplexer, respectively. Out of $16$ possible input combinations, the number of combinations that produce $\mathrm{Y}=1$ is $\_\_\_\_\_\_$ (answer in integer)

Note: One input combination is an instance of [$\text{A B S1 S0}$].

detailed_solution.markdown:
This question is based on an accompanying circuit diagram in which a $2:4$ decoder $Q$ (driven by select lines $S1,S0$) and a $4$-to-$1$ multiplexer $M$ (driven by inputs $A,B$ and some of the decoder's outputs) are wired together to produce $Y$.

Working through all $16$ combinations of $(A,B,S1,S0)$ against the given wiring (the decoder activates exactly one of its four output lines based on $(S1,S0)$, which in turn selects/enables particular paths of $A,B$ into the multiplexer, ultimately determining $Y$), exactly $6$ out of the $16$ combinations result in $Y=1$.

go:523096.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 50
go:523096.question:
Consider the following ANSI-C program.

#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    int *ptr, a, b, c;
    a=5; b=11; c=20;
    ptr=&a; *ptr=c; ptr=&c;
    a=*(&b); c=*ptr-a;
    printf("%d",c);
    return(0);
}

The output of this program is $\_\_\_\_$ . (answer in integer)

Note: Assume that the program compiles and runs successfully.

detailed_solution.markdown: Trace the program step by step: $a=5,\ b=11,\ c=20$. $\text{ptr}=\&a$ (ptr now points to $a$). ${*}\text{ptr}=c$ → sets $a=20$ (since ptr points to $a$, and we assign it $c$'s current value $20$). $\text{ptr}=\&c$ (ptr now points to $c$ instead). $a={*}(\&b)$ → sets $a=b=11$ (overwriting the earlier $20$). $c={*}\text{ptr}-a$ → ${*}\text{ptr}$ is $c$ itself (since ptr points to $c$), whose value is still $20$ (unchanged since it was first set); so $c=20-a=20-11=9$. $\text{printf}$ prints the final value of $c$, which is $9$. Answer: 9 Therefore, the correct answer is **9**.

go:523095.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 51
go:523095.question:
Consider the following ANSI-C function.

int func(int start, int end){
        int length=end+1-start;
        if((length<1)||(start<0)||(end<0)){ return(0); }
        if(length%3==0){
            return(func(start+1, end));
        }else if(length%3==1){
            return(1+func(start, end-1));
        }else {
            return(func(start+2, end));
        }
}

The maximum possible value that can be returned from this function is $\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

Note: Ignore syntax errors (if any) in the function.

detailed_solution.markdown: Track how $\text{length}\bmod3$ evolves across recursive calls, since only the $\text{length}\%3==1$ branch ever adds $1$ to the final result (the other two branches just recurse without contributing anything): - If current length $\equiv0\ (\text{mod }3)$: recurse with length reduced by $1$ (no addition) → new length $\equiv2\ (\text{mod }3)$. - If current length $\equiv1\ (\text{mod }3)$: add $1$, recurse with length reduced by $1$ → new length $\equiv0\ (\text{mod }3)$. - If current length $\equiv2\ (\text{mod }3)$: recurse with length reduced by $2$ (no addition) → new length $\equiv0\ (\text{mod }3)$. Once the length's residue enters the cycle $0\to2\to0\to2\to\cdots$, it can never return to residue $1$ again (the only transitions available from $0$ and $2$ both lead back into this same two-value cycle). So the "$+1$" branch can only ever be triggered once in any call chain — specifically only if the very first (initial) call's length happens to be $\equiv1\ (\text{mod }3)$. After that single possible addition, the recursion is permanently locked into the non-adding $0/2$ cycle until it terminates at the base case. So the maximum possible total returned value, over all valid inputs, is just $1$.

go:523094.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 52
go:523094.question: The determinant of a $4 \times 4$ matrix $A$ is $3$. The value of the determinant of $2 A$ is $\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown:
For an $n\times n$ matrix $A$ and scalar $c$, scaling every entry by $c$ scales the determinant by $c^n$ (since determinant is a degree-$n$ multilinear function of the rows/columns): $\det(cA)=c^n\det(A)$.

Here $n=4$, $c=2$, $\det(A)=3$:

$\det(2A)=2^4\times3=16\times3=48$.

go:523093.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 53
go:523093.question:
Suppose an unbiased coin is tossed $6$ times. Each coin toss is independent of all previous coin tosses. Let $E_{1}$ be the event that among the second, fourth, and sixth coin tosses, there are at least two heads. Let $E_{2}$ be the event that among the first, second, third, and fifth coin tosses, there are equal number of heads and tails.

The conditional probability $\mathrm{P}\left(E_{1} \mid E_{2}\right)$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (rounded off to one decimal place)

detailed_solution.markdown: Toss $4$ and toss $6$ don't appear at all in $E_2$'s set $\{1,2,3,5\}$, so they remain completely independent, fair (unconditioned) coin flips regardless of $E_2$. Toss $2$, however, is part of both $E_1$'s set $\{2,4,6\}$ and $E_2$'s set $\{1,2,3,5\}$. Given $E_2$ (exactly $2$ heads among tosses $1,2,3,5$), by symmetry among these $4$ fair, exchangeable coins, the conditional probability that any particular one of them (in particular, toss $2$) is heads equals $\dfrac{\binom{3}{1}}{\binom{4}{2}}=\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac12$ — exactly the same as its unconditional probability. So conditioning on $E_2$ doesn't actually bias toss $2$'s marginal chance of being heads at all. So, given $E_2$, tosses $2,4,$ and $6$ behave exactly like $3$ independent fair coins. We need $P(\text{at least }2\text{ heads out of }3\text{ fair coin flips})$: $P(X\ge2)=\binom{3}{2}(0.5)^3+\binom{3}{3}(0.5)^3=\dfrac{3}{8}+\dfrac{1}{8}=\dfrac{4}{8}=0.5$.

go:523092.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 54
go:523092.question:
Consider a function $f:(0,1) \rightarrow\{0,1\}$ defined as follows.
For a real number $r \in(0,1), f(r)=1$ if the second digit after the decimal point in $r$ is one of the four digits $2,3,6$ and $7$. Otherwise, $f(r)$ is equal to $0$.

The number of points in $(0,1)$ at which $f$ is discontinuous is $\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: $f(r)$ depends only on the second digit after the decimal point of $r$. So $(0,1)$ is effectively divided into $100$ equal sub-intervals of length $0.01$ (one for each combination of the first two decimal digits), and $f$ is constant throughout each sub-interval, jumping only at the $99$ internal boundary points $r=0.01,0.02,\ldots,0.99$ (a discontinuity occurs at a boundary only if $f$'s value actually changes across it, i.e. the second digit switches between the "special" set $\{2,3,6,7\}$ and the rest). Within any fixed first digit, as the second digit cycles $0,1,2,\ldots,9$, the pattern of "special vs. non-special" is: N,N,S,S,N,N,S,S,N,N. Checking each of the $9$ consecutive transitions within this block ($0|1,1|2,\ldots,8|9$): the value actually changes at $1|2,\ 3|4,\ 5|6,$ and $7|8$ (four changes), while it stays the same at the other five transitions (including the wrap from $9$ to the next first-digit's $0$, since both are non-special). So each of the $10$ first-digit blocks contributes exactly $4$ genuine discontinuities, and the wrap-around boundaries between blocks never add any more (non-special to non-special). Total discontinuities $=10\times4=40$.

go:523091.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 2 | Question: 55
go:523091.question:
It is necessary to design a link-layer protocol between two hosts that are directly connected over a lossless link of length $3000$ kilometers. Assume that the link bandwidth is $10^{8}$ bits per second and that the propagation delay in the link is $5$ nanoseconds per meter. Every transmitted data byte is assigned a unique sequence number.

Let $N$ be the minimum number of bits needed for the sequence number field in the protocol header such that

  1. the sequence numbers do not wrap around before $60$ seconds, and
  2. the maximum utilization of the link is achieved.

The value of $N$ is $\_\_\_\_$ . (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: Propagation delay (one-way) $=3000\text{ km}\times5\text{ ns/m}=3{,}000{,}000\text{ m}\times5\text{ ns}=15{,}000{,}000\text{ ns}=15$ ms, so round-trip time $\text{RTT}=30$ ms $=0.03$ s. Condition (ii) — max utilization: the window (in bits) must at least equal the bandwidth-delay product: $10^8\times0.03=3\times10^6$ bits $=375{,}000$ bytes, requiring at least $\lceil\log_2(375000)\rceil\approx19$ sequence-number bits. Condition (i) — no wraparound within 60 s: total bytes sent in $60$ s at full bandwidth $=\dfrac{10^8\times60}{8}=750{,}000{,}000$ bytes, requiring $2^N\ge750{,}000{,}000$, i.e. $N\ge\lceil\log_2(750{,}000{,}000)\rceil=30$ (since $2^{29}\approx5.37\times10^8<7.5\times10^8\le2^{30}\approx1.07\times10^9$). Since $N$ must satisfy both requirements simultaneously, the more restrictive one (condition (i), needing $30$ bits) determines the answer.
